imagine you're at the arcade and you buy a bunch of ticket-multiplier tokens. the more tokens people buy, the more the arcade manager has to buy physical prizes to keep up so they don't get trapped. 

gamma exposure is that exact arcade panic, but for the stock market. 

big options dealers sell calls and puts to gamblers. to stay safe and not lose their shirts when the price moves, those dealers have to constantly buy or sell the actual underlying stock to stay "delta neutral"—meaning they hedge every bet. 

when dealers are sitting on massive gamma (usually right around huge options expiration dates):
- if the stock ticks **up**, dealers are forced to **buy** more stock to cover their exposure, which pushes the price higher.
- if it ticks **down**, they have to **sell**, which greases the slide downward.

it's basically a giant cushion that holds the market in place, right until someone pops it and everything accelerates violently.
